etymology: From the APCO "ten-codes," numeric shorthand for police radio developed in the late 1930s by Charles Hopper of the Illinois State Police and adopted by the Association of Public-Safety Communications Officials; 10-4 = "message received, acknowledged." Truckers took the codes onto Citizens Band radio, and when the 1974 national 55-mph speed limit and the fuel crisis set off the CB craze of 1975–77, 10-4, good buddy became a national catchphrase, fixed in place by C.W. McCall’s "Convoy" (No. 1, January 1976) and Smokey and the Bandit (1977).
biblical_def: 10-4, good buddy is the CB trucker’s sign-off: "message received, friend." In the mid-1970s every station wagon had a CB, every kid had a "handle," and half of America was saying it. The Christian observation: the phrase holds two small virtues worth teaching a child. The first is the plain acknowledgement. 10-4 means I heard you, I understood, and I will act on it — no evasion, no ambiguity. Our Lord asked the same of every disciple’s speech: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mat 5:37). It is also the posture of a good listener, "swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19), and, at its highest, of young Samuel before God: "Speak; for thy servant heareth" (1Sa 3:10). The second virtue is the good buddy — the stranger on the highway who watched out for you, warned you of a wreck ahead, and called for help if you broke down at two in the morning. That road fellowship was a faint picture of what Proverbs commends: "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24). A grandparent who ran a CB in 1976 can teach a grandchild to say "10-4" to his parents with a cheerful heart — and can point him to the Friend who always has His radio on.
webster_summary: 1970s CB-radio sign-off (APCO ten-code 10-4, "message received") — a plain acknowledgement that models yea-yea, nay-nay speech (Mat 5:37) and the road friendship Proverbs commends (Pro 18:24).
webster_full: 10-4, GOOD BUDDY, phr. (CB-radio slang, 1970s; Boomer era) Message received and understood, friend; also a general "okay," "agreed," or friendly sign-off. 10-4 alone, "affirmative, acknowledged," remains in use.
Ten-code — the APCO numeric radio shorthand: 10-4 (acknowledged), 10-20 (location), 10-33 (emergency), 10-7 (out of service).
Good buddy — CB address for a fellow driver; from buddy, American, 1850s, probably from brother or butty (companion).
Decode for families: the CB was the 1970s group chat — with handles instead of usernames and the whole interstate listening.
scriptures: Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
corruption_summary: A harmless and even wholesome catchphrase; its only danger is the anonymity of the airwaves, where a handle could say what a name would not — the ancestor of the online troll.
corruption_paragraphs: Most of what the CB craze gave America was good fun and real help: stranded motorists found, wrecks reported, lonely night drivers kept awake. 10-4 is a model of clear speech, and the friendliness of good buddy was genuine. But the CB also taught a generation the strange freedom of the anonymous voice. Behind a handle, men said things on channel 19 they would never have said across a diner counter, and the airwaves filled with profanity and worse. The internet is that lesson at scale. The tongue that "no man can tame" is not tamed by being anonymous.

The Christian standard does not change with the medium. "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips" (Psa 141:3) applies to a microphone as much as to a mouth. And the friendship of the road points beyond itself to the "friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24) — who hears before we call.
roots_summary: APCO ten-codes (late 1930s, Illinois State Police) → truckers’ CB radio → 1975–77 CB craze; "Convoy" (1976), Smokey and the Bandit (1977).
roots_lines: Late 1930s: ten-codes devised by Charles Hopper, Illinois State Police; adopted by APCO
1958: the FCC opens the Citizens Band (11-meter) to the public
1974: national 55-mph limit and fuel crisis — truckers organize by CB
1975–77: CB craze; "Convoy" by C.W. McCall reaches No. 1 (January 1976)
Buddy — American, 1850s, a companion (perhaps from brother)
usage: "Dad asked if I took out the trash. I said ‘10-4, good buddy,’ and Grandpa laughed for five minutes."
Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay (Mat 5:37).
There is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother (Pro 18:24).

etymology: Citizens Band radio protocol of the 1960s–70s: a driver wishing to enter a busy channel "breaks" in by saying breaker, usually followed by the channel number ("Breaker one-nine" for channel 19, the truckers’ channel), and waits for the others to yield. Doubled for emphasis, breaker, breaker became one of the signature sounds of the 1975–77 CB craze and of the trucker films and songs it produced.
biblical_def: Breaker, breaker is how a CB user asked to break into a conversation already in progress: a polite interruption, a request for the floor. "Breaker one-nine, this here’s the Rubber Duck." The Christian observation: the phrase is a small lesson in courteous speech, and a large picture of prayer. On the radio, the man who wanted to speak announced himself and waited; the channel was shared, and you did not simply talk over everybody. That is the wisdom of Proverbs: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Pro 18:13). Our children live in a world of constant interruption, and the old CB courtesy is worth reviving: ask, wait, then speak. But the larger picture is this. Every believer has a channel that is never too busy. "Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not" (Jer 33:3). "Call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me" (Psa 50:15). God does not merely let us break in; He promises, "before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear" (Isa 65:24). No trucker on a lonely stretch at three in the morning ever had a channel like that.
webster_summary: 1970s CB-radio call to enter a busy channel ("Breaker one-nine") — a model of courteous speech (Pro 18:13) and a picture of prayer to the God who answers before we call (Isa 65:24).
webster_full: BREAKER, BREAKER, interj. (CB-radio slang, 1960s–70s; Boomer era) A call requesting permission to break into a channel and speak, usually followed by the channel number: "Breaker one-nine." Breaker (n.), one who breaks in on a channel.

Webster (1828) — BREAKER, noun The person who breaks any thing; a violator or transgressor; as a breaker of the law. 1. A rock which breaks the waves; or the wave itself which breaks the waves; or the wave itself which breaks against a rock, a sand bank, or the shore, exhibiting a white foam. 2. A pier, mound or other solid matter, placed in a river, to break the floating ice, and prevent it from injuring a bridge below; called also ice-breaker.
Decode for families: the CB rule was ask, wait, then speak. A good rule for the dinner table.
scriptures: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
Jer 33:3
Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.
And call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me.
And it shall come to pass, that before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.
Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips.
corruption_summary: Harmless radio etiquette; its lesson is courtesy, and its picture is prayer to the God whose channel is never busy.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in breaker, breaker itself. The CB code of courtesy — identify yourself, ask for the channel, yield to emergencies — was better than the manners of most modern comment sections. If anything, the phrase rebukes us. A generation that grew up asking for the floor has raised a generation that interrupts by default, in person and online. James’s rule — swift to hear, slow to speak — was easier to keep when the radio forced you to wait your turn.

The word breaker has an older meaning in Scripture: Micah’s "breaker," the One who goes up before His people and breaks open the way. The believer who calls on God does not merely break into a conversation; he is heard by the One who has already broken through every barrier between God and man. Psalm 141:3 is a fitting prayer before any microphone: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips."
roots_summary: Old English brecan (to break) → breaker → 1960s–70s CB protocol "breaker" / "breaker one-nine" → breaker, breaker.
roots_lines: Old English brecan — to break, to burst, to violate
Breaker — one who breaks; also a wave breaking on rocks (see Breaker)
1958: Citizens Band radio opened to the public by the FCC
1960s–70s: breaker — CB call to enter a channel; channel 19 the truckers’ channel
Scripture: Mic 2:13 — "The breaker is come up before them"
usage: "Breaker, breaker — can I say something before you two finish arguing?"
Call unto me, and I will answer thee (Jer 33:3).
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him (Pro 18:13).

etymology: From the APCO police ten-code 10-20, "location" (late 1930s), shortened on CB radio to twenty. What’s your 20? — "Where are you?" — was a staple of the 1970s CB craze, heard in "Convoy" (1975–76) and countless trucker films, and survives as a jokey way to ask someone’s whereabouts.
biblical_def: What’s your 20? means "Where are you?" — a CB trucker’s question to a fellow driver somewhere out on the interstate. A grandparent might still ask it on the phone. The Christian observation: it is the first question God asked of fallen man. After Adam sinned and hid among the trees, "the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?" (Gen 3:9). God was not lacking information; He was calling a sinner out of hiding. The question was mercy. Scripture is plain that no one can actually hide his 20 from God: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there" (Psa 139:7–8). "The eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good" (Pro 15:3). For the guilty, that is terrifying; for the lost child of God, it is the best news in the world. The Good Shepherd goes after the one sheep that is lost "until he find it." A father can turn the old CB joke into a lifelong question for his son: where are you, really — not on the map but before God? And he can promise him that wherever he ends up, his Father in heaven knows his 20 and is coming after him.
webster_summary: 1970s CB slang (APCO ten-code 10-20, "location") for "Where are you?" — the first question God asked fallen man (Gen 3:9), from whose presence no one can hide (Psa 139:7–8).
webster_full: WHAT’S YOUR 20?, phr. (CB-radio slang, 1970s; Boomer era) Where are you? What is your location? From the ten-code 10-20. Reply: "My 20 is mile marker 130 on I-95."
Twenty, n. (CB) One’s location.
Decode for families: before phone location-sharing, this was how you found a friend on the road.
scriptures: Gen 3:9
And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?
Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.
Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the LORD. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD.
Pro 15:3
The eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.
corruption_summary: A harmless CB question that echoes God’s first question to fallen man — "Where art thou?" — and the truth that no one can hide his location from the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing in the phrase needs correcting; its value is in what it recalls. The modern world has made what’s your 20 obsolete — every phone shares its location continuously — and yet people have never been better at hiding. We hide behind screens, behind busyness, behind curated images. Adam hid among the trees; we hide among the apps. "Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the LORD" (Jer 23:24).

The comfort is that God’s knowledge of our 20 is not surveillance but pursuit. The God who asked Adam "Where art thou?" is the God who came looking, and who in the fullness of time came all the way to us, to seek and to save that which was lost. A child who learns that God always knows where he is should learn in the same breath that God is always coming for him.
roots_lines: Late 1930s: APCO ten-codes for police radio; 10-20 = location
1960s–70s: truckers shorten it on CB to your 20
1975–77: CB craze makes "What’s your 20?" a national catchphrase
Hebrew ayyekah — "Where art thou?" (Gen 3:9)
Scripture: Psa 139:7–12 — no place hidden from God
usage: "Grandpa called and said, ‘What’s your 20?’ I said, ‘The Chick-fil-A on Route 3.’"
Where art thou? (Gen 3:9) — God’s first question, asked in mercy.
Whither shall I flee from thy presence? (Psa 139:7).

etymology: From Smokey Bear, the U.S. Forest Service’s fire-prevention mascot (1944), whose broad-brimmed campaign hat resembles the hats worn by many state highway patrols. CB truckers of the late 1960s–70s called a state trooper Smokey, Smokey Bear, or simply bear ("bear in the air" for a police aircraft, "Smokey with ears" for a trooper with a CB). The film Smokey and the Bandit (1977) fixed the word in national memory.
biblical_def: Smokey was CB-trucker slang for a state trooper — the man with the campaign hat and the radar gun. "Smokey’s taking pictures at the 112" meant there was a speed trap ahead, and every driver on the channel slowed down. The Christian observation: the word is affectionate as often as hostile, but the habit it fed — warning one another to dodge the law — deserves a moment’s thought. Scripture tells us exactly who Smokey is: "he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain" (Rom 13:4). "Rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same" (Rom 13:3). The driver who slows down only when Smokey is near has learned to fear the trooper but not to love the law; his obedience lasts exactly as long as the radar. That is the obedience of eye-service, and the Bible has a sharper word for it: "The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion" (Pro 28:1). A father who drives the limit with no Smokey in sight is teaching his children that righteousness does not depend on being watched. And there is a Watcher who never goes off shift: "be sure your sin will find you out" (Num 32:23).
webster_summary: 1970s CB slang (from Smokey Bear’s campaign hat) for a state trooper — the "minister of God" of Rom 13:4, whom the righteous need not dodge because they obey when no one is watching (Pro 28:1).
webster_full: SMOKEY, n. (CB-radio slang, late 1960s–70s; Boomer era) A state highway patrolman; any traffic police officer. Also Smokey Bear, bear. "Smokey’s got his picture-taker out" — a radar trap ahead. Bear in the air — a police aircraft.
Webster (1828) — SMOKY, adjective 1. Emitting smoke; fumid; as smoky fires. 2. Having the appearance or nature of smoke; as a smoky fog.
Decode for families: the respectful modern word is trooper or officer. Teach both, and teach Rom 13:4.
scriptures: Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Rom 13:3
For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same:
Rom 13:7
Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
But if ye will not do so, behold, ye have sinned against the LORD: and be sure your sin will find you out.
corruption_summary: The CB culture around Smokey turned law enforcement into a game of evasion; Scripture calls the officer God’s minister for good and asks for obedience that does not depend on being watched.
corruption_paragraphs: Smokey and the Bandit made the outlaw the hero and the sheriff the clown, and a generation cheered. The CB channel became a cooperative early-warning system for breaking the speed limit, and the trooper became the opponent in a game. That is a small thing, but small things train the conscience. A boy who learns that the law is something to outwit learns that what matters is not being caught. Romans 13 teaches the reverse: the magistrate is to be honored, his sword respected, and his laws kept "not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake."

The deeper lesson is about the One who sees. The trucker’s radio could warn him of every Smokey on the interstate, but no channel warns of God’s approach. "Be sure your sin will find you out" (Num 32:23). The righteous do not need a radar detector; they are "bold as a lion" (Pro 28:1), because they have nothing to flee. Render honor to whom honor is due (Rom 13:7) — including the man in the campaign hat.
roots_summary: Old English smoca (smoke) → Smokey Bear (U.S. Forest Service, 1944) → campaign-hat resemblance → late-1960s–70s CB Smokey (state trooper).
roots_lines: Old English smoca — smoke; smoky, full of smoke
1944: Smokey Bear, U.S. Forest Service fire-prevention mascot, in a ranger’s campaign hat
Late 1960s–70s CB slang: Smokey, bear — state trooper (same style of hat)
1977: Smokey and the Bandit (Burt Reynolds, Jackie Gleason)
Scripture: Rom 13:1–7 — the magistrate as minister of God
usage: "Grandpa still flashes his headlights to warn other drivers about Smokey. Dad says that’s not as innocent as it looks."
He is the minister of God to thee for good (Rom 13:4).
The wicked flee when no man pursueth (Pro 28:1).

etymology: Surfing slang from the longboard era of 1950s–60s Southern California and Hawaii: to walk to the front of the board and curl all ten toes over the nose while riding a wave (hang five, one foot). It became a byword of the early-1960s surf craze — Gidget (1959), the Beach Boys, Jan and Dean — and the name of the Hang Ten surfwear label (founded 1960) with its two-bare-footprints logo. It is used loosely for "relax, enjoy the ride."
biblical_def: To hang ten is to ride a surfboard with all ten toes over the nose — the most daring and graceful trick of the longboard era — and, by extension, to be cool, relaxed, and riding life’s wave with easy confidence. The Christian observation: the surfer’s joy in the sea is a creature’s joy in a good creation, and Scripture shares it. "So is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts. There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein" (Psa 104:25–26). God made a sea to be played in. There is "a time to laugh" and "a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4), and a boy on a board at dawn is not wasting his life. But the wave also teaches what no surfer can forget: he does not command the sea. "The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea" (Psa 93:4). The surfer rides by yielding to a power he cannot control, and the best of them have a deep respect, almost a fear, of the ocean. That is the right posture of a man before God: active, skilled, joyful, and humble before a might that could swallow him. "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still" (Psa 107:29). The one who hangs ten on God’s wave knows Whose wave it is.
webster_summary: Early-1960s surf slang for riding a longboard with all ten toes over the nose; loosely, to be cool and relaxed — a creature’s play in the sea God made (Psa 104:26), humbled by the LORD mightier than its waves (Psa 93:4).
webster_full: HANG TEN, v. phr. (surfing slang, 1950s–60s; Boomer era) To ride a surfboard with the toes of both feet curled over its front edge. Hence, informally, to relax and enjoy oneself. Hang five — the same with one foot.

Webster (1828) — HANG, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive hanged or hung. 1. To suspend; to fasten to some fixed object above, in such a manner as to swing or move; as, to hang a thief. Pharaoh hanged the chief baker. Hence, 2. To put to death by suspending by the neck. Many men would rebel, rather than be ruined; but they would rather not rebel than be hanged. 3. To place without any solid support or foundation. He hangeth the earth upon nothing. Job 36:1 .
Decode for families: the surf culture of the early 1960s was the sunny, mostly innocent prelude to the counterculture — beach movies, harmonies, and woodies.
scriptures: So is this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts.
There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein.
Psa 93:4
The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea.
Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
corruption_summary: Surf slang is largely innocent; the culture around it drifted toward making the wave and the leisure life an end in themselves, where Scripture makes the sea a gift and its Maker the joy.
corruption_paragraphs: The early surf craze was mostly clean fun, and a Christian need not frown at it. The danger lay downstream. By the later 1960s surf culture had become, for some, a whole philosophy: drop out, chase the perfect wave, live for the endless summer. The sea became an idol, and the surfer a kind of monk of leisure. Scripture does not condemn the board or the beach. It condemns the heart that makes any created good the center of its life.

The psalmists loved the sea precisely because it pointed past itself. Its waves are mighty; the LORD is mightier (Psa 93:4). Its storms terrify; He makes them calm (Psa 107:29). A father who surfs with his son can make every session a lesson in creaturely joy and creaturely humility. Ride the wave; thank its Maker; and never forget who is holding the ocean.
roots_summary: Old English hangian (to hang) + ten (toes) → 1950s–60s longboard surfing hang ten / hang five → 1960 Hang Ten label → loose sense "relax."
roots_lines: Old English hangian — to hang, to be suspended
1950s–60s California and Hawaii: hang ten, hang five — noseriding tricks on a longboard
1959: Gidget launches the surf craze in film
1960: Hang Ten surf apparel founded; two-footprint logo
Scripture: the sea as God’s playground and God’s servant (Psa 104:26; Psa 93:4)
usage: "Grandpa says he could hang ten at Huntington Beach in ’63. Grandma says he could hang two."
There is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein (Psa 104:26).
The LORD on high is mightier than the mighty waves of the sea (Psa 93:4).

etymology: Wipe out, to destroy utterly or obliterate, is centuries old (compare the KJV "I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish"). Southern California surfers of the early 1960s used wipeout for a spectacular fall from the board, and the Surfaris’ instrumental "Wipe Out" (recorded 1962, a hit in 1963), with its maniacal laugh and drum solo, carried the word to every teenager in America. By the 1970s it meant any crash or crushing failure, and wiped out meant exhausted.
biblical_def: A wipeout is a crash: in surfing, a violent fall that sends the board flying and the surfer under; in life, any spectacular failure. To be wiped out is to be utterly exhausted. The Christian observation: everyone wipes out, and Scripture is realistic about it and hopeful in it. Peter’s great wipeout happened on water. He walked toward the Lord, "But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me" (Mat 14:30), and Jesus immediately stretched forth His hand. That is the gospel pattern. "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16). "Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand" (Psa 37:24). The prophet speaks for every believer who has crashed hard: "Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me" (Mic 7:8). But the older sense of wipe out is sobering too. God once said of Jerusalem in judgment, "I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down" (2Ki 21:13). There is a wipeout from which no one rises except by grace — and grace has made a way. A father can tell his son after his worst failure: you wiped out; you are not wiped out. "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee" (Isa 43:2).
webster_summary: Early-1960s surf slang (the Surfaris’ "Wipe Out," 1963) for a violent fall from the board, hence any crash or failure — answered by the Lord who catches sinking Peter (Mat 14:30) and raises the just man seven times (Pro 24:16).
webster_full: WIPEOUT, n. (surfing slang, early 1960s; Boomer era) A fall from a surfboard, especially a violent one; hence any crash, defeat, or complete failure. WIPE OUT, v. To fall from the board; to crash. Wiped out, adj., exhausted.

Webster (1828) — WIPE, verb transitive 1. To rub something soft for cleaning; to clean by rubbing; as, to wipe the hands or face with a towel. Luke 7:38 . 2. To strike off gently. Some natral tears they droppd, but wipd them soon. 3. To cleanse from evil practices or abuses; to overturn and destroy what is foul and hateful. I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish. 2 Kings 21:13 . 4. To cheat; to defraud. To wipe away, to cleanse by rubbing or tersion; as, to wipe away a stain or reproach. To wipe off, to clear away. wipe off this foul stain; wipe off the dust. To wipe out, to efface; to obliterate. wipe out the blot.
Older and still-current sense: to wipe out, to destroy completely, to obliterate (2Ki 21:13).
scriptures: But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.
For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.
Isa 43:2

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
corruption_summary: A largely innocent word; Scripture adds the truth that every believer falls and is upheld, and that there is a final wiping-out from which only grace delivers.
corruption_paragraphs: The surfer’s wipeout was half a boast. The bigger the wave, the bigger the wipeout, and a good one earned respect on the beach. There is something healthy in that: a culture that is not afraid of failure is braver than one that is. Scripture’s saints are full of wipeouts — Abraham lying about Sarah, Moses striking the rock, David on the rooftop, Peter by the fire — and none of them is hidden. The Bible does not airbrush its heroes because its hero is God, who lifts up the fallen.

The danger is the opposite lesson, which our age teaches loudly: that failure defines you, that one public wipeout ends a life. Micah answers it: "when I fall, I shall arise" (Mic 7:8). And the Lord Jesus answers it with His hand outstretched to a sinking disciple (Mat 14:30). The only wipeout to fear is the last one, the judgment that wipes a city like a dish (2Ki 21:13) — and Christ bore that for His people.
roots_summary: Old English wípian (to wipe) + out → wipe out (obliterate, centuries old) → early-1960s surf wipeout → 1963 Surfaris hit → general "crash, failure."
roots_lines: Old English wípian — to wipe, to rub clean
Wipe out — to efface, to destroy utterly; KJV 2Ki 21:13, "wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish"
Early 1960s Southern California surf slang: wipeout — a fall from the board
1963: the Surfaris’ "Wipe Out" reaches the Top 10
1970s–present: wipeout — any crash or failure; wiped out — exhausted
usage: "I totally wiped out on my bike." "You fell; you’re not finished. Get up."
A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again (Pro 24:16).
Lord, save me (Mat 14:30) — the best prayer after a wipeout.

etymology: Southern California surf slang of the late 1950s and early 1960s, of uncertain origin (perhaps from "Ho, Dad!" or the beatnik address Daddy-O). A hodad was a non-surfer who hung around the beach acting the part — the bleached hair, the baggies, the board on the car roof — but never paddled out; also a show-off or tough guy who made trouble on the sand. The word was used in the surf movies and magazines of the craze.
biblical_def: A hodad was a beach poser: a guy with all the surfer gear and none of the surfing, who wanted the image without the work and the risk. Real surfers despised him. The Christian observation: the hodad is a figure Scripture knows well, and Our Lord’s sharpest words are reserved for the religious version of him. Of the Pharisees He said, "all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments" (Mat 23:5) — the gear without the waves. "Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them" (Mat 6:1). James presses it home: "be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves" (Jas 1:22). There is a churchgoing hodad who has the Bible on the dashboard, the T-shirt, the vocabulary, the right opinions, and has never paddled out into the cold water of obedience. Proverbs describes the type: "There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing" (Pro 13:7). A father can use the old surf word to ask his son, and himself, a searching question: am I a surfer or a hodad? Do I actually do the thing, or do I only look like someone who does?
webster_summary: Early-1960s surf slang (origin uncertain) for a beach poser with the gear but not the skill — the type Our Lord rebuked in those who do all their works "to be seen of men" (Mat 23:5).
webster_full: HODAD, n. (surf slang, late 1950s–60s; Boomer era) A non-surfer who frequents the beach and affects surf style without surfing; a poser. Also, a beach show-off or troublemaker. Also spelled hodaddy.
Compare poser, wannabe, gremmie / gremlin (a young beginner, sometimes a nuisance).
Decode for families: the modern hodad posts the gym selfie and skips the workout.
scriptures: Mat 23:5
But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments,
Mat 6:1
Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Pro 13:7
There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches.
Mat 6:2

Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
corruption_summary: The hodad wanted the image without the substance; Scripture names the religious hodad a hypocrite and calls for doers of the word, not hearers only (Jas 1:22).
corruption_paragraphs: The surfers who mocked hodads were onto something true: image without reality is contemptible. But the culture as a whole was drifting toward the hodad. The surf look sold far more boards than the surf ever saw, and by the 1970s millions dressed the part of a life they did not live. Our image-saturated age has perfected the hodad. Social media rewards the appearance of the thing over the thing itself.

Our Lord’s word for the religious hodad was hypocrite — originally a stage actor behind a mask. "They have their reward" (Mat 6:2), He said: the applause they wanted is all they get. The Christian life cannot be posed. It is paddling out, every day, into the cold water of actual obedience — and finding the Lord already there.
roots_summary: Late-1950s Southern California surf slang hodad (origin uncertain; perhaps "Ho, Dad!" or Daddy-O) → early-1960s surf-craze vocabulary.

Late 1950s: surf slang for a beach poser or troublemaker
Early 1960s: in surf magazines and beach movies of the craze
Greek hypokritēs — a stage actor; Our Lord’s word for the religious poser (Mat 6:2)
Scripture: Mat 23:5 — "for to be seen of men"
usage: "Grandpa says he was a surfer. Great-Uncle Ed says he was a hodad with a nice board."
All their works they do for to be seen of men (Mat 23:5).

etymology: From crash, a loud violent noise or collision (Middle English crasschen, imitative). The slang sense — to sleep, especially to bed down somewhere temporary ("can I crash at your place?") — is American, recorded from the mid-twentieth century and universal in 1960s hippie usage, alongside crash (to fall asleep from exhaustion, or to come down hard from a drug high) and crash pad. It is still everyday English for sleeping over.
biblical_def: To crash is to sleep — usually somewhere temporary, on a couch or a floor, after a long day or a long night. "Can I crash at your place?" was the hippie’s request on the road, and it is still a college student’s. The Christian observation: the word carries two good things and one warning. The first good thing is sleep itself, which God gives as a gift and a sign of trust: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me" (Psa 3:5) — written by David while fleeing Absalom, sleeping rough. The second is hospitality, which Scripture commands: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Heb 13:2); "Use hospitality one to another without grudging" (1Pe 4:9). A Christian home ought to be the kind of place where a young person in trouble can crash. Our Lord Himself knew what it was to have nowhere: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head" (Luk 9:58). The warning lies in the drug sense: to crash is also to come down hard after a high, and the 1960s used one word for both because for many the two were the same. The believer’s sleep is not a collapse after excess but a rest in God’s keeping. Open your couch; guard your house; and sleep like David, sustained by the LORD.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (mid-20th c., universal in 1960s hippie usage) for sleeping, especially somewhere temporary; also to collapse after a drug high — Scripture blesses the sleep the LORD sustains (Psa 3:5) and the hospitality that offers the couch (Heb 13:2).
webster_full: CRASH, v.i. (slang, mid-20th c.; universal in Boomer and later usage) 1. To sleep, especially in a temporary place: "You can crash on the couch." 2. To fall asleep suddenly from exhaustion. 3. To come down abruptly from a drug-induced high. 4. To attend uninvited: to crash a party (1920s).
Webster (1828) — CRASH, noun The loud mingled sound of many things falling and breaking at once; as the sound of a large tree falling and its branches breaking, or the sound of a falling house.
Related: crashing (the noise of destruction, Zep 1:10); crash pad (a place to sleep).
scriptures: Psa 3:5
I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
Luk 9:58
And Jesus said unto him, Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Psa 4:8
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
corruption_summary: Crash joins honest sleep and open-hearted hospitality to the hard landing after a drug high; Scripture blesses the first two and calls the believer to sleep in trust, not to collapse after excess.
corruption_paragraphs: The hippie road ran on couches. Young people hitchhiked across the country trusting that someone would let them crash, and many were taken in by kindness — and many by predators. Hospitality without discernment became a trap, especially for runaway girls. The Christian command to entertain strangers was never a command to abandon prudence; Lot’s house shows how dangerous an open door in a wicked city can be, and the wise householder protects those under his roof.

The other sense of crash — coming down hard — names the rhythm of a life built on highs. The stimulant lifts and drops; the binge ends in collapse; the weekend ends in a crash. God’s rhythm is different: work and rest, six days and one, evening and morning. "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety" (Psa 4:8). That is not crashing; it is resting.
roots_summary: Middle English crasschen (imitative: to break with a loud noise) → crash (collision) → mid-20th-c. slang crash (to sleep; to come down) → 1960s crash pad.

Crash (n.) — a loud sudden noise; a collision (see Crashing, Zep 1:10)

1960s drug slang: crash — the abrupt end of a high
usage: "Can my friend crash here tonight? His parents are out of town."
I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me (Psa 3:5).

etymology: Crash (to sleep, slang) + pad (one’s bed or lodging, 1930s jazz slang, from the older sense of a bundle of straw to lie on). A crash pad — an apartment or house where anyone could sleep for free, often on mattresses covering the floor — was a fixture of the mid-1960s counterculture, especially in Haight-Ashbury and the East Village during 1966–68, when runaways poured into both. Airline crews later used crash pad for a shared apartment near a base.
biblical_def: A crash pad was a hippie flophouse: an apartment where anyone could sleep, mattresses wall to wall, the door always open. In 1967 there were hundreds in San Francisco and New York, filled with runaways, drifters, and the predators who followed them. The Christian observation: the crash pad was a counterfeit of something God intends — a home for the homeless — built without the one thing that makes a home safe. Scripture says, "God setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6). The young people who flocked to the crash pads had often fled real families, some of them cruel, and were looking for belonging. What they found instead was a room without a father: no one in charge, no one responsible, no protection for the weak. Proverbs saw the danger: "As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place" (Pro 27:8), and "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners" (1Co 15:33). The story that fits is the prodigal’s. In the far country, with the crash-pad friends gone, "when he came to himself, he said ... I will arise and go to my father" (Luk 15:17–18). The Christian answer to the crash pad is not a locked door but a household with a father in it — a church and a home with room at the table, where "the solitary" are set "in families" and the lost can come home.
webster_summary: Mid-1960s counterculture slang for a communal apartment where anyone could sleep free — a counterfeit home without a father, answered by the God who setteth the solitary in families (Psa 68:6).
webster_full: CRASH PAD, n. (Boomer slang, mid-1960s) A house or apartment providing free, temporary sleeping space, typically on floor mattresses, for transients and runaways; hence any place to stay temporarily. Later, a shared lodging for airline crews.
Webster (1828) — PAD, noun A soft saddle, cushion or bolster stuffed with straw, hair or other soft substance.
Pad (1930s jazz slang) — one’s bed or home (see Pad).
scriptures: Psa 68:6
God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.
Pro 27:8
As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place.
Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!
I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee,
corruption_summary: The crash pad offered belonging without authority and shelter without protection; Scripture’s answer is the household with a father in it, where God sets the solitary in families.
corruption_paragraphs: The crash pad was idealistic: share everything, own nothing, welcome all. It failed for the reason every fatherless arrangement fails. Without anyone responsible, the strongest took what they wanted and the weakest paid. Reports from the Haight in 1967 tell of runaway girls exploited within days of arriving, of hepatitis and malnutrition, of drugs pushed on children. Belonging without authority is not freedom; it is exposure.

The church has a better answer and has not always given it. The prodigals of 1967 needed doors that were open and houses that were ordered — love and law together. That is what a Christian home is meant to be, and what a congregation is meant to be for those who have no home. God "setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6), and He does it, very often, through families who have made room.
roots_summary: Crash (slang, to sleep) + pad (1930s jazz, a bed or home; from pad, a bundle of straw) → mid-1960s crash pad, Haight-Ashbury and East Village.

etymology: From pit (Old English pytt, Latin puteus, a well or hole). The pits, meaning the very worst, is American slang recorded from the 1950s and very common from the late 1960s and 1970s ("This job is the pits"); its origin is debated — perhaps the bottom of a pit, perhaps a shortening of armpits, perhaps the orchestra pit or a cockpit. Older senses survive in the pit as a name for hell and the pits at a racetrack.
biblical_def: The pits means the worst — the bottom, the most miserable situation imaginable. "Being grounded over spring break is the pits." The Christian observation: Scripture knows the pit far better than the slang does, and it knows the way out. The pit in the Bible is the place of the lowest humiliation and danger. Joseph’s brothers "took him, and cast him into a pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it" (Gen 37:24). Jeremiah was let down into a cistern where "there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire" (Jer 38:6). And the pit is a name for death and the grave itself: "thou hast kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit" (Psa 30:3). But the pit is never the last word for God’s people. David’s testimony is the testimony of every saved sinner: "He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings" (Psa 40:2). Joseph went from the pit to the palace. Jeremiah was drawn up by an Ethiopian with old rags and ropes. The Lord Jesus went down into the deepest pit of all, death itself, and came up again. A child who says his day was the pits can be taught, kindly, that he has not yet seen the pit — and that the God of Psalm 40 has never yet lost anyone in one.
webster_summary: Boomer-era slang (1950s; common from the late 1960s) for the very worst situation — a light echo of the biblical pit of humiliation and death, out of which the LORD brings His people and sets their feet upon a rock (Psa 40:2).
webster_full: THE PITS, n. pl. (Boomer slang, 1950s–present) The worst possible situation, place, or thing; something extremely unpleasant. "Monday mornings are the pits."

Webster (1828) — PIT, n. 1. An artificial cavity made in the earth, narrow compared with its depth; distinguished from a well in being generally larger. 2. A deep place; an abyss; profundity. 3. The grave. 4. The shaft of a mine.
Decode for families: one of the most durable Boomer words; your children understand it without translation.
scriptures: Psa 40:2
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.
And they took him, and cast him into a pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it.
Jer 38:6

Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.
Psa 30:3
O LORD, thou hast brought up my soul from the grave: thou hast kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit.
Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.
corruption_summary: A harmless exaggeration in everyday speech; Scripture fills the word with real depth — the pit of humiliation, death, and the grave — and with the real rescue of the God who draws His people up.
corruption_paragraphs: The slang trivializes a weighty word, as slang does. Most things called "the pits" are inconveniences. That is not a sin, but it is worth noticing, because a generation that calls a cancelled concert "the pits" has little vocabulary left for genuine affliction. Scripture’s pit is a dry cistern with a boy in it, sold by his brothers; a prophet sinking in mud; the mouth of the grave.

Proverbs adds a moral note: "Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein" (Pro 26:27). Many of the pits we fall into are ones we dug. But even those are not beyond the reach of the God who "brought me up also out of an horrible pit" (Psa 40:2). The gospel is the story of a rescue from the lowest place, by One who went down there Himself.

etymology: From bummer (a disappointing experience, mid-1960s; originally a bad drug trip, a "bum trip"), and bum, worthless or bad (American, 19th century, from bummer, a loafer, probably from German Bummler, an idler). Bummed or bummed out — disappointed, depressed — is recorded from the late 1960s and remains standard casual English.
biblical_def: To be bummed or bummed out is to be disappointed, let down, mildly depressed. "I’m bummed we can’t go to the beach." The Christian observation: the word names a real emotion and invites a real conversation. Scripture never tells a believer he must not feel downcast. The psalmist talks to his own soul about it: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance" (Psa 42:5). Elijah, after his greatest victory, sat under a juniper tree and said, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life" (1Ki 19:4) — and God’s first response was to give him food and sleep. So a Christian parent can take a child’s "I’m bummed" seriously. But Scripture also teaches the soul to answer its disappointment. Paul "learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11) — learned, which means it can be taught. He could say, "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair" (2Co 4:8). And Habakkuk gives the believer’s defiant joy: though the fig tree does not blossom and the fields yield nothing, "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation" (Hab 3:18). Bummed is a feeling. Hope is a decision about where to look.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (late 1960s, from bummer) for disappointed or downcast — a feeling Scripture takes seriously (Psa 42:5; 1Ki 19:4) and answers with learned contentment (Php 4:11) and hope in God (Hab 3:18).
webster_full: BUMMED, adj. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–present) Disappointed, dejected, mildly depressed. Also bummed out. "She was bummed about the rain." Compare bummer (n.), a disappointment; bum (adj.), poor, worthless ("a bum deal").
Decode for families: a low-intensity word for sadness. Listen for whether it is really low-intensity.
scriptures: Psa 42:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.

But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die; and said, It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.
Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;
Hab 3:17

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
Hab 3:18
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
corruption_summary: Bummed names disappointment casually and can make discontent a habit; Scripture takes the downcast soul seriously and teaches it to answer itself with hope in God.
corruption_paragraphs: The danger in bummed is not the word but the habit. A culture that is always slightly bummed — about the weather, the game, the job, the news — has made discontent its resting state. Israel in the wilderness was bummed about the manna, and Scripture calls that murmuring. Paul’s contentment was not natural to him; he "learned" it (Php 4:11), and it can be learned by a child too, beginning with thanksgiving for small things.

At the same time, a parent must listen carefully, because bummed is often the word a young person uses when he has no better word for something heavier. Elijah’s juniper tree (1Ki 19:4) was real despair, and God met it with food, sleep, and a still small voice before He gave Elijah new work. The Christian answer to sadness is never "cheer up" but "hope thou in God" (Psa 42:5) — spoken alongside, with patience.
roots_summary: German Bummler (an idler) → American bummer (a loafer, 1850s) → bum (worthless) → mid-1960s bummer, bum trip → late-1960s bummed (out).

1850s–60s American: bummer — a loafer; a Civil War forager

Mid-1960s drug slang: bum trip, bummer — a bad trip; any disappointment
Late 1960s: bummed, bummed out — disappointed, dejected
usage: "I’m bummed we lost." "Me too. Want to talk about it, or want a milkshake first?"
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? hope thou in God (Psa 42:5).
I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content (Php 4:11).

etymology: From the verb sell out: to dispose of all one’s stock (17th century), and in American political slang of the nineteenth century, to betray a cause or party for gain. The noun sellout for such a betrayal, and for the betrayer, became a favorite insult of the 1960s counterculture, hurled at musicians who signed with big labels, activists who took establishment jobs, and anyone who traded ideals for money or comfort. A sellout is also, separately, an event with every ticket sold.
biblical_def: A sellout is a person who abandons his principles for money, fame, or comfort — the folk singer who goes commercial, the radical who joins the corporation. In 1968 it was the worst thing one hippie could call another. The Christian observation: the insult names a real sin, and Scripture records its two great examples. Esau "for one morsel of meat sold his birthright" (Heb 12:16), trading what was eternal for what was immediate. And Judas went to the chief priests and "said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver" (Mat 26:15). Our Lord put the whole matter in one question: "For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mar 8:36). Paul named the root: "the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows" (1Ti 6:10). But the counterculture’s use of the word had a blind spot. It called a young man a sellout for taking a job, marrying, and supporting a family — that is, for growing up. Scripture calls that faithfulness. The real sellout is not the man who works for a living but the man who sells the truth. A father can teach his son the difference: never sell your soul, your conscience, or your Lord; and never be ashamed of honest work.
webster_summary: Boomer counterculture insult for one who betrays principles for money or comfort — the sin of Esau (Heb 12:16) and Judas (Mat 26:15), though the hippie wrongly applied it to honest work and family duty.
webster_full: SELLOUT, n. (Boomer slang, 1960s–present; from 19th-c. political sell out) 1. A person who betrays principles, a cause, or a community for personal gain. 2. The act of such a betrayal. 3. (unrelated) An event for which all tickets are sold. v. to sell out.

Webster (1828) — SELL, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive sold . [ 1. To transfer property or the exclusive right of possession to another for an equivalent in money. It is correlative to buy , as one party buys what the other sells . It is distinguished from exchange or barter , in which one commodity is given for another; wheras in selling the consideration is money, or its representative in current notes. To this distinction there may be certain exceptions. ’Esau sold his birthright to Jacob for a mess of pottage.’ But this is unusual. ’Let us sell Joseph to the Ishmaelites- And they sold him for twenty pieces of silver.’ Genesis 37:27 . Among the Hebrews, parents had power to sell their children. 2. To betray; to deliver or surrender for money or reward; as, to sell one’s country. 3. To yield or give for a certain consideration. the troops fought like lions, and sold their lives dearly.
Decode for families: ask what a person is being accused of selling. If it is his conscience, the charge is grave. If it is his time for a paycheck, it is not a charge at all.
scriptures: And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
Mar 8:36
For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
And Jacob said, Swear to me this day; and he sware unto him: and he sold his birthright unto Jacob.
corruption_summary: The counterculture rightly despised betrayal for gain but wrongly called ordinary responsibility a sellout; Scripture condemns selling the soul and honors honest work.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation has its sellouts, and the Boomer generation coined the word for them with real moral passion. It was right to despise the artist who wrote what sold rather than what was true, and the activist who abandoned the poor for a comfortable office. That is Esau’s profanity and Judas’s silver. But the word was used too widely. It became a weapon against anyone who chose stability over rebellion, and it taught a generation to despise the ordinary virtues — showing up, paying bills, raising children — that hold a society together. Paul’s counsel to work with one’s own hands is not selling out; it is the gospel lived on a Tuesday.

The irony of the word is that many who used it most loudly in 1968 sold out most completely later — not by getting jobs but by abandoning every conviction they had once held, including the true ones. The only way not to sell out is to belong to Someone who cannot be bought. The believer has been bought already, "not with corruptible things, as silver and gold," but with the precious blood of Christ.
